passages.title: Lord Ashby's Speech
passages.text: Lord Ashby rose to address the council. 'I have always supported the expansion of the eastern market,' he began, glancing briefly at the merchants' guild, whose banner hung above his seat. 'Of course, I would never let personal interest cloud my judgement.' Several councillors exchanged looks. One quietly noted that Ashby's brother-in-law had recently bought most of the land beside the proposed site.

questions.q: What is implied about Lord Ashby?
options: He may have a conflict of interest.
He is completely neutral about the market.
He secretly opposes the market expansion.
The merchants' guild strongly dislikes him.
questions.explain: His relative owns land beside the site — he could profit.

questions.q: What do the councillors' exchanged looks suggest?
options: They doubt his sincerity.
They agree enthusiastically.
They are confused about the market.
They are bored.
questions.explain: A silent reaction to his claim of no personal interest.

questions.q: Why does the writer include the final sentence?
options: to give a reason to question his motives
to show that his family is very wealthy
to describe the land beside the market site
to praise Ashby for being open and honest
questions.explain: It undercuts his claim about 'personal interest'.

passages.title: On Letters
passages.text: It is tempting to see the decline of handwritten letters as a simple loss. Yet letters were never merely vessels of affection; they were also instruments of control, used to issue orders, settle debts and, occasionally, to deceive. What we mourn, perhaps, is not the letter itself but the slowness it imposed — a slowness that forced writers to weigh their words. Digital messages need not be careless, but their speed makes carelessness easy.

questions.q: What is the writer's main point?
options: What we miss is the slowness that encouraged careful thought.
Letters were always affectionate, unlike the messages we send today.
Digital messages are always careless, so they cannot replace letters.
We should stop using digital messages and return to writing letters.
questions.explain: 'What we mourn… is the slowness… that forced writers to weigh their words.'

questions.q: What does 'instruments of control' suggest about letters?
options: They were also used for power and practical business.
They were difficult and slow for most people to write.
They were controlled and read by the government.
They were a kind of music played on instruments.
questions.explain: Orders, debts, deception — not just affection.

questions.q: What is the writer's attitude to digital messages?
options: balanced: not bad in themselves, but speed invites carelessness
entirely negative: digital messages have destroyed careful writing
entirely positive: speed has made communication better in every way
indifferent: the writer has no real view on digital messages
questions.explain: 'Need not be careless, but… carelessness easy.'

passages.title: The Carriage Debate
passages.text: Councillor Reyes: 'Banning carriages from the old town will revitalise the area — look at what happened in Lindhaven.' Councillor Mbeki: 'Lindhaven had a railway connecting it to every village. We have one muddy road. Without an alternative, you're not revitalising the old town — you're isolating it.'

questions.q: What is Mbeki's main objection?
options: The two towns aren't comparable without other transport.
Carriages are cheap and popular with old-town visitors.
The carriage ban actually failed badly in Lindhaven.
The old town is thriving and doesn't need any help.
questions.explain: He attacks the comparison: Lindhaven had a railway.

questions.q: Which part of Reyes' reasoning does Mbeki challenge?
options: the analogy with Lindhaven
the cost of the ban
the safety of carriages
the history of the old town
questions.explain: Reyes argues by analogy; Mbeki shows the analogy is weak.

questions.q: Which would most strengthen Reyes' case?
options: evidence that a new transport link will be built
proof that Lindhaven is popular with tourists
proof that carriages are noisy and dangerous
photos showing how beautiful the old town is
questions.explain: It removes Mbeki's objection directly.

passages.title: Streamlining
passages.text: When the new head librarian announced that she was 'streamlining the collection', staff were initially relieved; the shelves had long been overcrowded. By spring, however, entire sections on local history had vanished, and the archive room was being refurbished as a private meeting space for the board. Requests for clarification were met with assurances that 'everything valuable has been preserved digitally'. Nobody could say who had decided what counted as valuable.

questions.q: What does the passage suggest about 'streamlining'?
options: It was a euphemism for removing important material.
It was a popular change that every member of staff welcomed.
It simply meant tidying the overcrowded shelves.
It referred to a long-planned technology upgrade.
questions.explain: Whole sections vanished — far beyond tidying.

questions.q: What is the writer's attitude?
options: critical and sceptical
warmly admiring
completely neutral
amused and light-hearted
questions.explain: Quotation marks and the final sentence signal doubt.

questions.q: What does the final sentence highlight?
options: a lack of accountability
a technical failure in the archive
incompetence among the library staff
how popular the board has become
questions.explain: No one knows who decided — nobody is responsible.

passages.title: The Tin Box
passages.text: Grandfather never spoke about the war. But every November he polished a small tin box until it shone, and every November he put it back, unopened, on the highest shelf. After he died, we found inside only a ribbon and a photograph of a young man none of us recognised, signed 'Until we meet again — T.'

questions.q: What can we infer about the box?
options: It had deep personal significance.
It was worthless to him after the war.
He had forgotten what was inside it.
It contained the medals he had won.
questions.explain: A yearly ritual shows it mattered deeply.

questions.q: Why did he polish the box but never open it?
options: The memories were probably too painful.
The box was locked and he had lost the key.
He was saving it to sell after the war.
He didn't know there was anything inside.
questions.explain: He cared for it but avoided its contents.

questions.q: Who was the young man most likely to be?
options: someone close to him, possibly lost in the war
Grandfather himself as a young soldier
a famous actor Grandfather admired
the narrator's father before he married
questions.explain: Signed 'T.' to Grandfather; 'Until we meet again' suggests loss.

passages.title: The Cartographer's Dilemma
passages.text: When the Royal Society commissioned a new map of the kingdom, it expected precision. What it received was something more troubling. The cartographer, a meticulous woman named Orla Venn, had walked every road herself and discovered that several villages shown on the old maps no longer existed, while others had grown into towns that appeared nowhere. Worse, three 'rivers' turned out to be dry ditches, drawn decades earlier to strengthen land claims. Venn's map was accurate, but it was also politically explosive: it undermined the boundaries on which several noble estates depended. The Society shelved it for a generation. Her story is a reminder that maps are never merely descriptive; they are arguments about who owns the world.

questions.q: What did Venn find out about the old maps?
options: Some features had been invented for land claims.
They were more accurate than the Society thought.
They had been copied from foreign maps.
They left out the kingdom's largest towns entirely.
questions.explain: Three 'rivers' were dry ditches drawn 'to strengthen land claims'.

questions.q: Why was her map shelved?
options: It threatened powerful landowners.
It contained serious measuring errors.
She refused to let the Society publish it.
It was too expensive to print in colour.
questions.explain: It 'undermined the boundaries on which several noble estates depended'.

questions.q: What is the writer's main point?
options: Maps reflect power as well as geography.
Old maps should never be trusted at all.
Cartographers should avoid politics completely.
The Royal Society was right to be careful.
questions.explain: 'Maps are never merely descriptive; they are arguments about who owns the world.'

passages.title: In Praise of Boredom
passages.text: We have engineered boredom out of our lives. Every queue, commute and pause is now filled by a glowing screen. Yet psychologists increasingly argue that boredom is not a malfunction but a signal: a prompt to seek something more meaningful. In one study, participants who had first completed a dull task, copying numbers from a phone directory, went on to generate more creative uses for a plastic cup than those who had not. The researchers do not claim that tedium is pleasant, only that it may be productive. The difficulty is that the payoff comes later, while the discomfort is immediate, and a phone offers instant relief.

questions.q: How do psychologists view boredom, according to the text?
options: as a useful signal
as a harmless habit
as a sign of illness
as a modern invention
questions.explain: 'Boredom is not a malfunction but a signal.'

questions.q: What did the study suggest?
options: A dull task first can boost creativity.
Phone directories are useful for memory.
Creative people rarely feel bored at all.
Plastic cups make tasks less boring.
questions.explain: Those who did the dull task produced more creative ideas.

questions.q: Why do people avoid boredom, in the writer's view?
options: The benefit is delayed but the discomfort isn't.
Psychologists have told them it is dangerous.
Boredom always makes people less productive.
Modern jobs leave no time to feel bored.
questions.explain: 'The payoff comes later, while the discomfort is immediate.'
